claim: Brief (2-3d) monocular deprivation (MD) during the critical period induces a profound loss of responsiveness within binocular (V1b) and monocular (V1m) regions of rodent primary visual cortex.
source: Brief (2-3d) monocular deprivation (MD) during the critical period induces a profound loss of responsiveness within binocular (V1b) and monocular (V1m) regions of rodent primary visual cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with established findings in the field.

claim: Loss of responsiveness after brief MD has largely been ascribed to long-term depression (LTD) at thalamocortical synapses.
source: This has largely been ascribed to long-term depression (LTD) at thalamocortical synapses, while a contribution from intracortical inhibition has been controversial.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field as described in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Despite depression at thalamocortical synapses, thalamocortical E-I ratio was unaffected in V1b following brief MD.
source: Despite depression at thalamocortical synapses, thalamocortical E-I ratio was unaffected in V1b and shifted toward excitation in V1m, indicating that thalamocortical excitation was not effectively reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F showing no significant change in E-I ratio in V1b (p = 0.80).

claim: Thalamocortical E-I ratio shifted toward excitation in V1m following brief MD.
source: Despite depression at thalamocortical synapses, thalamocortical E-I ratio was unaffected in V1b and shifted toward excitation in V1m, indicating that thalamocortical excitation was not effectively reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G demonstrating a significant increase in E-I ratio in V1m (p = 0.0063).

claim: Feedback intracortical E-I ratio was shifted toward inhibition in V1m following brief MD.
source: In contrast, feedback intracortical E-I ratio was shifted toward inhibition in V1m, and a computational model demonstrated that these opposing shifts produced an overall suppression of layer 4 excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F demonstrating a significant decrease in intracortical E-I ratio (p = 0.022).

claim: Opposing shifts in feedforward and feedback E-I ratios produced an overall suppression of layer 4 excitability.
source: In contrast, feedback intracortical E-I ratio was shifted toward inhibition in V1m, and a computational model demonstrated that these opposing shifts produced an overall suppression of layer 4 excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9.

claim: Feedforward and feedback E-I ratios can be independently tuned by visual experience.
source: Thus, feedforward and feedback E-I ratios can be independently tuned by visual experience, and enhanced feedback inhibition is the primary driving force behind loss of visual responsiveness.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing opposite changes in feedforward vs feedback E-I ratios.

claim: Enhanced feedback inhibition is the primary driving force behind loss of visual responsiveness following brief MD.
source: Thus, feedforward and feedback E-I ratios can be independently tuned by visual experience, and enhanced feedback inhibition is the primary driving force behind loss of visual responsiveness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combination of experimental data and computational modeling showing that intracortical changes dominate over thalamocortical changes.

claim: The critical period in rats and mice extends from roughly postnatal days 21–35.
source: In the visual system of rats and mice, the critical period extends from roughly postnatal days 21–35 (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), when visual deprivation has catastrophic effects on visual function, including loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye (Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004), reduced visual acuity (Fagiolini et al., 1994), loss of tuning to many stimulus characteristics (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), and a suppression of firing within primary visual cortex (V1) (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Espinosa and Stryker, 2012.

claim: Visual deprivation during the critical period causes loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye.
source: In the visual system of rats and mice, the critical period extends from roughly postnatal days 21–35 (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), when visual deprivation has catastrophic effects on visual function, including loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye (Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004), reduced visual acuity (Fagiolini et al., 1994), loss of tuning to many stimulus characteristics (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), and a suppression of firing within primary visual cortex (V1) (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heynen et al., 2003 and Frenkel and Bear, 2004.

claim: Visual deprivation during the critical period causes reduced visual acuity.
source: In the visual system of rats and mice, the critical period extends from roughly postnatal days 21–35 (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), when visual deprivation has catastrophic effects on visual function, including loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye (Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004), reduced visual acuity (Fagiolini et al., 1994), loss of tuning to many stimulus characteristics (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), and a suppression of firing within primary visual cortex (V1) (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fagiolini et al., 1994.

claim: Visual deprivation during the critical period causes suppression of firing within primary visual cortex (V1).
source: In the visual system of rats and mice, the critical period extends from roughly postnatal days 21–35 (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), when visual deprivation has catastrophic effects on visual function, including loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye (Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004), reduced visual acuity (Fagiolini et al., 1994), loss of tuning to many stimulus characteristics (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012), and a suppression of firing within primary visual cortex (V1) (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hengen et al., 2013 and Hengen et al., 2016.

claim: Brief (1–3 days) monocular deprivation during the critical period induces a rapid loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye in both binocular (V1b) and monocular (V1m) regions of V1.
source: Even very brief (1–3 days) monocular deprivation (MD) during the critical period induces a rapid loss of visual responsiveness to the deprived eye in both binocular (V1b, Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004) and monocular (V1m; Heynen et al., 2003; Kaneko et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011) regions of V1.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Heynen et al., 2003; Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Kaneko et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The rapid loss of deprived-eye responsiveness is thought to be primarily cortical in origin.
source: This rapid loss of deprived-eye responsiveness is thought to be primarily cortical in origin (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Gainey and Feldman, 2017; Sommeijer et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011), but it remains controversial which forms of intracortical plasticity underlie it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Gainey and Feldman, 2017; Sommeijer et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Brief MD induces LTD at excitatory synapses onto pyramidal neurons.
source: Traditionally, the loss of visual responsiveness after brief MD has been ascribed to LTD at excitatory synapses onto pyramidal neurons (Crozier et al., 2007; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heynen et al., 2003; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Smith et al., 2009), including LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto excitatory neurons in layer 4 (Crozier et al., 2007; Khibnik et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Crozier et al., 2007; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heynen et al., 2003; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Smith et al., 2009.

claim: Brief MD induces LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto excitatory neurons in layer 4.
source: Traditionally, the loss of visual responsiveness after brief MD has been ascribed to LTD at excitatory synapses onto pyramidal neurons (Crozier et al., 2007; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heynen et al., 2003; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Smith et al., 2009), including LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto excitatory neurons in layer 4 (Crozier et al., 2007; Khibnik et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crozier et al., 2007; Khibnik et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Cortical inhibitory circuitry is plastic and can be modified by brief MD.
source: In contrast, a number of recent studies have demonstrated that cortical inhibitory circuitry is also plastic and can be modified by brief MD (Kannan et al., 2016; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2006; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kannan et al., 2016; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2006; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014; Sun et al., 2016.

claim: The relationship between excitation (E) and inhibition (I) is critically important for neocortical information processing.
source: Given that the relationship between excitation (E) and inhibition (I) is critically important for neocortical information processing (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Haider and McCormick, 2009), E-I ratio is likely a more relevant measure of circuit excitability than excitation alone (House et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011 and Haider and McCormick, 2009.

claim: E-I ratio is likely a more relevant measure of circuit excitability than excitation alone.
source: Given that the relationship between excitation (E) and inhibition (I) is critically important for neocortical information processing (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Haider and McCormick, 2009), E-I ratio is likely a more relevant measure of circuit excitability than excitation alone (House et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to House et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2014.

claim: Sensory information is relayed to cortex via thalamocortical inputs, which excite both excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons within layer 4, forming a 'feedforward' circuit.
source: Sensory information is relayed to cortex via thalamocortical inputs, which excite both excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons within layer 4, forming a 'feedforward' circuit.
evidence: This is a description of established neocortical circuit architecture.

claim: Pyramidal neurons recurrently excite other pyramidal neurons and interneurons within layer 4, forming an intracortical 'feedback' circuit.
source: In addition, pyramidal neurons recurrently excite other pyramidal neurons and interneurons within layer 4, forming an intracortical 'feedback' circuit.
evidence: This is a description of established neocortical circuit architecture.

claim: Feedforward and feedback circuits provide separable contributions to sensory-evoked cortical activity.
source: While these two circuits are intimately related and share both excitatory and inhibitory elements, they ultimately provide separable contributions to sensory-evoked cortical activity (Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reinhold et al., 2015.

claim: Feedback recurrent inputs greatly outnumber feedforward thalamocortical inputs.
source: Furthermore, feedback recurrent inputs greatly outnumber feedforward thalamocortical inputs (Ahmed et al., 1994; Bopp et al., 2017; Douglas et al., 1989), suggesting that the layer 4 feedback circuit is poised to disproportionately affect network excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 1994; Bopp et al., 2017; Douglas et al., 1989.

claim: The layer 4 feedback circuit is poised to disproportionately affect network excitability.
source: Furthermore, feedback recurrent inputs greatly outnumber feedforward thalamocortical inputs (Ahmed et al., 1994; Bopp et al., 2017; Douglas et al., 1989), suggesting that the layer 4 feedback circuit is poised to disproportionately affect network excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the numerical dominance of feedback inputs.

claim: Paired monosynaptic EPSCs versus disynaptic IPSCs scaled linearly at different stimulus intensities.
source: Paired monosynaptic EPSCs versus disynaptic IPSCs scaled linearly at different stimulus intensities (Figure 1E, inset), indicating that thalamocortical E-I ratio is conserved as additional thalamocortical axons are recruited.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E inset demonstrating linear scaling (R2 = 0.90).

claim: Thalamocortical E-I ratio is conserved as additional thalamocortical axons are recruited.
source: Paired monosynaptic EPSCs versus disynaptic IPSCs scaled linearly at different stimulus intensities (Figure 1E, inset), indicating that thalamocortical E-I ratio is conserved as additional thalamocortical axons are recruited.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear scaling of E and I with stimulus intensity.

claim: Evoked thalamocortical EPSC kinetics and peak latency were unchanged following perfusion of TTX+4-AP.
source: At the stimulus intensities used, evoked thalamocortical EPSC kinetics and peak latency were unchanged following perfusion of TTX+4-AP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, control peak latency = 10.5 ± 0.27 ms, TTX+4-AP peak latency = 10.6 ± 0.28 ms, p = 0.82), while IPSCs were completely abolished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, control peak amplitude = 1320 ± 164 pA, TTX+4-AP peak amplitude = 15 ± 4 pA, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical comparison (p = 0.82).

claim: IPSCs were completely abolished following perfusion of TTX+4-AP.
source: At the stimulus intensities used, evoked thalamocortical EPSC kinetics and peak latency were unchanged following perfusion of TTX+4-AP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, control peak latency = 10.5 ± 0.27 ms, TTX+4-AP peak latency = 10.6 ± 0.28 ms, p = 0.82), while IPSCs were completely abolished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, control peak amplitude = 1320 ± 164 pA, TTX+4-AP peak amplitude = 15 ± 4 pA, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D with statistical comparison (p < 0.01).

claim: Evoked EPSCs represent monosynaptic thalamocortical inputs.
source: Hence, evoked EPSCs represent monosynaptic thalamocortical inputs, and evoked IPSCs represent disynaptic inputs from local inhibitory interneurons driven by thalamocortical activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX+4-AP experiments showing EPSCs are preserved while IPSCs are abolished.

claim: Evoked IPSCs represent disynaptic inputs from local inhibitory interneurons driven by thalamocortical activation.
source: Hence, evoked EPSCs represent monosynaptic thalamocortical inputs, and evoked IPSCs represent disynaptic inputs from local inhibitory interneurons driven by thalamocortical activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX+4-AP experiments showing IPSCs are abolished, indicating they require action potentials in interneurons.

claim: Brief MD induces a modest but significant reduction in evoked thalamocortical quantal amplitude.
source: Brief MD induced a modest but significant reduction in evoked thalamocortical quantal amplitude (Figure 2C, control = 10.7 pA ± 0.35 pA, deprived = 9.7 pA ± 0.20 pA, p < 0.05), without any impact on input resistance, resting membrane potential (Figure 2D), waveform kinetics (Figure 2E), or spontaneous mEPSC amplitudes (which are enriched for intracortical excitatory synapses, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical comparison (p < 0.05).

claim: Brief MD has no impact on input resistance or resting membrane potential of layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
source: Brief MD induced a modest but significant reduction in evoked thalamocortical quantal amplitude (Figure 2C, control = 10.7 pA ± 0.35 pA, deprived = 9.7 pA ± 0.20 pA, p < 0.05), without any impact on input resistance, resting membrane potential (Figure 2D), waveform kinetics (Figure 2E), or spontaneous mEPSC amplitudes (which are enriched for intracortical excitatory synapses, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D showing no significant differences.

claim: Brief MD has no impact on thalamocortical quantal event waveform kinetics.
source: Brief MD induced a modest but significant reduction in evoked thalamocortical quantal amplitude (Figure 2C, control = 10.7 pA ± 0.35 pA, deprived = 9.7 pA ± 0.20 pA, p < 0.05), without any impact on input resistance, resting membrane potential (Figure 2D), waveform kinetics (Figure 2E), or spontaneous mEPSC amplitudes (which are enriched for intracortical excitatory synapses, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E showing overlapping waveforms.

claim: Brief MD has no impact on spontaneous mEPSC amplitudes.
source: Brief MD induced a modest but significant reduction in evoked thalamocortical quantal amplitude (Figure 2C, control = 10.7 pA ± 0.35 pA, deprived = 9.7 pA ± 0.20 pA, p < 0.05), without any impact on input resistance, resting membrane potential (Figure 2D), waveform kinetics (Figure 2E), or spontaneous mEPSC amplitudes (which are enriched for intracortical excitatory synapses, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing no significant difference (p = 0.17).

claim: The reduction in thalamocortical quantal amplitude following brief MD is consistent with the induction of a postsynaptic depression selectively at thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
source: This reduction in quantal amplitude following brief MD is consistent with the induction of a postsynaptic depression selectively at thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective reduction in thalamocortical quantal amplitude without changes in spontaneous mEPSCs.

claim: Control neurons exhibited sustained depression of evoked thalamocortical EPSCs following LTD induction (64.4 ± 6.7% of baseline amplitude).
source: By pairing 1 Hz activation of thalamocortical axons with brief postsynaptic depolarization to −50 mV (in voltage clamp) for 10 min, we reliably induced sustained depression of evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto control neurons (Figure 3A,B,E, 64.4 ± 6.7% of baseline amplitude).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, E.

claim: Deprived neurons exhibited significantly less depression following LTD induction (89.3 ± 9.7% of baseline amplitude).
source: In contrast, deprived neurons exhibited significantly less depression following LTD induction (Figure 3B,F,G, 89.3 ± 9.7% of baseline amplitude, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, F, G with statistical comparison (p = 0.042).

claim: Brief MD induces a postsynaptic LTD-like depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
source: Taken together with the change in thalamocortical quantal amplitude, this strongly suggests that brief MD induces a postsynaptic LTD-like depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of reduced quantal amplitude and occlusion of LTD induction.

claim: There is a concurrent and even greater weakening of thalamocortical-recruited feedforward inhibition onto pyramidal neurons following brief MD.
source: Coupled with our previous result that thalamocortical-evoked E-I ratio is shifted toward excitation following brief MD (Figure 1G), this implies that there is a concurrent and even greater weakening of thalamocortical-recruited feedforward inhibition onto pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of thalamocortical LTD and increased E-I ratio.

claim: PV+ interneurons receive much stronger thalamic drive than SST+ interneurons.
source: PV+ interneurons receive much stronger thalamic drive than SST+ interneurons (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016), suggesting that they mediate the vast majority of thalamocortical-evoked feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016.

claim: PV+ interneurons mediate the vast majority of thalamocortical-evoked feedforward inhibition.
source: PV+ interneurons receive much stronger thalamic drive than SST+ interneurons (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016), suggesting that they mediate the vast majority of thalamocortical-evoked feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger thalamic drive to PV+ interneurons.

claim: PV+ interneurons fired readily even to modest thalamocortical stimulation and with a much lower threshold than pyramidal neurons.
source: Indeed, PV+ interneurons fired readily even to modest thalamocortical stimulation and with a much lower threshold than pyramidal neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, p < 0.0001), suggesting that these neurons contribute substantially to the feedforward E-I measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical comparison (p < 0.0001).

claim: PV+ interneurons contribute substantially to the feedforward E-I measurements.
source: Indeed, PV+ interneurons fired readily even to modest thalamocortical stimulation and with a much lower threshold than pyramidal neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, p < 0.0001), suggesting that these neurons contribute substantially to the feedforward E-I measurements.
evidence: This is inferred from the low firing threshold of PV+ interneurons to thalamocortical stimulation.

claim: Evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto PV+ interneurons were larger with faster kinetics than EPSCs onto pyramidal neurons.
source: Evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto PV+ interneurons were larger with faster kinetics than EPSCs onto pyramidal neurons as expected (Figure 4C; Hull et al., 2009; Kloc and Maffei, 2014), and EPSC amplitude onto the two cell types scaled linearly with stimulus intensity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Hull et al., 2009 and Kloc and Maffei, 2014.

claim: EPSC amplitude onto PV+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons scaled linearly with stimulus intensity.
source: Evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto PV+ interneurons were larger with faster kinetics than EPSCs onto pyramidal neurons as expected (Figure 4C; Hull et al., 2009; Kloc and Maffei, 2014), and EPSC amplitude onto the two cell types scaled linearly with stimulus intensity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D demonstrating linear relationship (R2 = 0.82).

claim: After brief MD, evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto PV+ interneurons were significantly smaller relative to paired neighboring pyramidal neurons.
source: After brief MD, evoked thalamocortical EPSCs onto PV+ interneurons were significantly smaller relative to paired neighboring pyramidal neurons (Figure 4E), resulting in an increase in thalamocortical-evoked pyramidal/PV EPSC charge ratio (Figure 4F, control ratio = 0.260 ± 0.027, deprived ratio = 0.369 ± 0.034, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F with statistical comparison (p = 0.0103).

claim: Brief MD induces a greater depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 PV+ interneurons than onto neighboring pyramidal neurons.
source: These data show that brief MD induces a greater depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 PV+ interneurons than onto neighboring pyramidal neurons; this in turn should reduce the ability of thalamocortical stimulation to recruit PV-mediated inhibition onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons and thus is predicted to contribute to the increased thalamocortical-evoked E-I ratio we observed.
evidence: This is directly supported by the paired recording data showing differential depression.

claim: Differential depression of thalamocortical synapses onto PV+ interneurons should reduce the ability of thalamocortical stimulation to recruit PV-mediated inhibition onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
source: These data show that brief MD induces a greater depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 PV+ interneurons than onto neighboring pyramidal neurons; this in turn should reduce the ability of thalamocortical stimulation to recruit PV-mediated inhibition onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons and thus is predicted to contribute to the increased thalamocortical-evoked E-I ratio we observed.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the observed differential depression.

claim: There was no significant difference in firing rate between deprived and control PV+ interneurons at any current injection.
source: There was no significant difference in firing rate between deprived and control PV+ interneurons at any current injection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B showing overlapping F-I curves.

claim: There was no difference in input resistance or rheobase of PV+ interneurons following brief MD.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in input resistance or rheobase (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pyramidal intrinsic excitability, input resistance, and rheobase were unaffected by brief MD.
source: Similarly, pyramidal intrinsic excitability, input resistance, and rheobase were unaffected by brief MD (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Unitary synaptic strength varied greatly at PV+ to pyramidal synapses (from 10's of pA to more than a nA).
source: Because unitary synaptic strength varied greatly at PV+ to pyramidal synapses (from 10's of pA to more than a nA, Figure 6D), we required a relatively high-throughput means to probe changes in strength at this synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Spike-evoked unitary IPSCs and optogenetically evoked putative unitary IPSCs were indistinguishable.
source: By patching onto the same PV+ interneuron we had stimulated optogenetically, we could show that spike-evoked unitary IPSCs and optogenetically evoked putative unitary IPSCs were indistinguishable (Figure 6C), indicating that this approach generates reliable estimates of unitary connection strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C showing overlapping traces.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean amplitude or distribution of IPSC amplitudes from PV+ interneurons to pyramidal neurons between control and deprived conditions.
source: Comparing optogenetically evoked putative unitary IPSC amplitude between control and deprived neurons revealed no significant difference in mean amplitude (control amplitude = 209 ± 29 pA, deprived amplitude = 215 ± 42 pA, p = 0.73), or in the distribution of IPSC amplitudes (p = 0.90), between conditions (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and 6E with statistical comparisons (p = 0.73 and p = 0.90).

claim: Changes in unitary synaptic strength from PV+ interneurons to pyramidal neurons do not significantly contribute to the weakening of thalamocortical-recruited inhibition following brief MD.
source: Hence, changes in unitary synaptic strength from PV+ interneurons to pyramidal neurons do not significantly contribute to the weakening of thalamocortical-recruited inhibition following brief MD.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in PV+ to pyramidal synaptic strength.

claim: The major factor that increases feedforward thalamocortical E-I ratio onto pyramidal neurons is the disproportionate reduction in thalamic drive to PV+ interneurons.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the major factor that increases feedforward thalamocortical E-I ratio onto pyramidal neurons is the disproportionate reduction in thalamic drive to PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of findings showing differential thalamocortical depression and no change in PV+ to pyramidal synapses or intrinsic excitability.

claim: 2–3 d of MD reduces visual responsiveness in V1m.
source: It is well established that 2–3 d of MD reduces visual responsiveness (Heynen et al., 2003; Kaneko et al., 2008), signal propagation (Wang et al., 2011), and firing rates (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016) in V1m.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heynen et al., 2003 and Kaneko et al., 2008.

claim: 2–3 d of MD reduces signal propagation in V1m.
source: It is well established that 2–3 d of MD reduces visual responsiveness (Heynen et al., 2003; Kaneko et al., 2008), signal propagation (Wang et al., 2011), and firing rates (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016) in V1m.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: 2–3 d of MD reduces firing rates in V1m.
source: It is well established that 2–3 d of MD reduces visual responsiveness (Heynen et al., 2003; Kaneko et al., 2008), signal propagation (Wang et al., 2011), and firing rates (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016) in V1m.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hengen et al., 2013 and Hengen et al., 2016.

claim: Intracortical excitatory synapses outnumber thalamocortical synapses by a factor of ~5 in neocortical layer 4.
source: Since intracortical excitatory synapses outnumber thalamocortical synapses by a factor of ~5 in neocortical layer 4 (Bopp et al., 2017) and by at least a factor of 2 onto PV+ interneurons (Kameda et al., 2012), a change in intracortical E-I ratio could potentially outweigh changes in thalamocortical circuitry to suppress excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bopp et al., 2017.

claim: Intracortical excitatory synapses outnumber thalamocortical synapses by at least a factor of 2 onto PV+ interneurons.
source: Since intracortical excitatory synapses outnumber thalamocortical synapses by a factor of ~5 in neocortical layer 4 (Bopp et al., 2017) and by at least a factor of 2 onto PV+ interneurons (Kameda et al., 2012), a change in intracortical E-I ratio could potentially outweigh changes in thalamocortical circuitry to suppress excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kameda et al., 2012.

claim: A change in intracortical E-I ratio could potentially outweigh changes in thalamocortical circuitry to suppress excitability.
source: Since intracortical excitatory synapses outnumber thalamocortical synapses by a factor of ~5 in neocortical layer 4 (Bopp et al., 2017) and by at least a factor of 2 onto PV+ interneurons (Kameda et al., 2012), a change in intracortical E-I ratio could potentially outweigh changes in thalamocortical circuitry to suppress excitability.
evidence: This is inferred from the numerical dominance of intracortical synapses.

claim: Following perfusion of DNQX, IPSCs were abolished.
source: Following perfusion of DNQX, IPSCs were abolished (Figure 7E, baseline IPSC amplitude = 909 ± 57 pA, DNQX IPSC amplitude = 12.2 ± 3.8 pA, p < 0.0001), indicating that ChR2-tdTomato expression was restricted to excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E with statistical comparison (p < 0.0001).

claim: ChR2-tdTomato expression was restricted to excitatory neurons.
source: Following perfusion of DNQX, IPSCs were abolished (Figure 7E, baseline IPSC amplitude = 909 ± 57 pA, DNQX IPSC amplitude = 12.2 ± 3.8 pA, p < 0.0001), indicating that ChR2-tdTomato expression was restricted to excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the abolition of IPSCs by DNQX, which blocks excitatory transmission.

claim: After brief MD, intracortical-evoked E-I ratios were significantly shifted toward greater inhibition in deprived versus control pyramidal neurons.
source: After brief MD, intracortical-evoked E-I ratios were significantly shifted toward greater inhibition in deprived versus control pyramidal neurons (Figure 7F, control ratio = 0.091 ± 0.009, deprived ratio = 0.066 ± 0.005, p < 0.05), with no accompanying change in passive properties (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F with statistical comparison (p = 0.022).

claim: Intracortical and thalamocortical E-I ratios were indistinguishable under control conditions.
source: Interestingly, intracortical and thalamocortical E-I ratios were indistinguishable under control conditions, but diverged dramatically after brief MD (Figure 7H, p < 0.0001, thalamocortical E-I values re-plotted from Figure 3C for comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H with statistical comparison (p = 0.84 for control).

claim: Intracortical and thalamocortical E-I ratios diverged dramatically after brief MD.
source: Interestingly, intracortical and thalamocortical E-I ratios were indistinguishable under control conditions, but diverged dramatically after brief MD (Figure 7H, p < 0.0001, thalamocortical E-I values re-plotted from Figure 3C for comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H with statistical comparison (p = 4.1×10−5 for deprived).

claim: Baseline E-I ratios are strongly conserved across feedforward and feedback microcircuits in layer 4 but can be inversely regulated by brief visual deprivation.
source: This suggests that baseline E-I ratios are strongly conserved across feedforward and feedback microcircuits in layer 4 but can be inversely regulated by brief visual deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that control E-I ratios are similar but deprived E-I ratios diverge.

claim: PV+ interneuron synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons are unaffected by brief MD.
source: PV+ interneuron synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons are unaffected by brief MD (Figure 6), allowing us to rule out a change at this synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was no significant change in the quantal amplitude of spontaneous mEPSCs onto pyramidal neurons after brief MD.
source: Further, we found no significant change in the quantal amplitude of spontaneous mEPSCs (enriched for intracortical synapses) onto pyramidal neurons after brief MD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that there is no postsynaptic depression of pyramidal-to-pyramidal synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is no postsynaptic depression of pyramidal-to-pyramidal synapses following brief MD.
source: Further, we found no significant change in the quantal amplitude of spontaneous mEPSCs (enriched for intracortical synapses) onto pyramidal neurons after brief MD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that there is no postsynaptic depression of pyramidal-to-pyramidal synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in spontaneous mEPSC amplitude.

claim: Brief MD has been shown to potentiate synapses from pyramidal neurons onto fast-spiking (FS) interneurons in layer 4.
source: Brief MD has previously been shown to potentiate synapses from pyramidal neurons onto fast-spiking (FS) interneurons in layer 4 (Maffei et al., 2006), so to test for postsynaptic strengthening of excitatory synapses onto PV+ FS interneurons, we targeted PV+ interneurons for whole-cell recording as described above (Figure 4B), and recorded spontaneous mEPSCs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maffei et al., 2006.

claim: Spontaneous mEPSC amplitude was increased in PV+ interneurons following brief MD.
source: Spontaneous mEPSC amplitude was increased following brief MD (Figure 8B, control amplitude = 15.8 ± 0.39 pA, deprived amplitude = 17.2 ± 0.54 pA, p < 0.05), while mEPSC frequency was unaffected (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B with statistical comparison (p = 0.044).

claim: mEPSC frequency in PV+ interneurons was unaffected by brief MD.
source: Spontaneous mEPSC amplitude was increased following brief MD (Figure 8B, control amplitude = 15.8 ± 0.39 pA, deprived amplitude = 17.2 ± 0.54 pA, p < 0.05), while mEPSC frequency was unaffected (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C with statistical comparison (p = 0.86).

claim: There was a decrease in mEPSC decay time in PV+ interneurons following brief MD.
source: There was a decrease in mEPSC decay time (Figure 8D,E; control Tau = 0.910 ± 0.024 ms, deprived Tau = 0.779 ± 0.035 ms, p < 0.01), with no change in passive properties (Rin, p = 0.33).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and 8E with statistical comparison (p = 0.003).

claim: One major factor that reduces intracortical E-I ratio following brief MD is enhanced excitation from nearby pyramidal neurons onto PV+ interneurons.
source: This suggests that one major factor that reduces intracortical E-I ratio following brief MD is enhanced excitation from nearby pyramidal neurons onto PV+ interneurons, either via modification to or insertion of kinetically faster synaptic AMPA receptors at these synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased mEPSC amplitude and faster kinetics in PV+ interneurons.

claim: The net effect of synaptic modifications following brief MD is predicted to increase thalamocortical E-I ratio while reducing intracortical E-I ratio.
source: In Figure 8F, we summarize the changes observed at thalamocortical and intracortical synapses in layer 4 following brief MD: the net effect of these synaptic modifications is predicted to increase thalamocortical E-I ratio while reducing intracortical E-I ratio, as we observed.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The shift in the intracortical E-I ratio in favor of inhibition dominates over the shift of thalamocortical E-I ratio in favor of excitation.
source: Hence, our model suggests that the shift in the intracortical E-I ratio in favor of inhibition dominates over the shift of thalamocortical E-I ratio in favor of excitation and is the key factor driving a reduction in V1m activity after brief MD.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9.

claim: The shift in intracortical E-I ratio is the key factor driving a reduction in V1m activity after brief MD.
source: Hence, our model suggests that the shift in the intracortical E-I ratio in favor of inhibition dominates over the shift of thalamocortical E-I ratio in favor of excitation and is the key factor driving a reduction in V1m activity after brief MD.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9.

claim: Brief MD does not render the thalamocortical circuit less excitable.
source: Surprisingly – despite confirming the induction of LTD at thalamocortical synapses in layer 4 – we find here that the E-I ratio of feedforward thalamocortical drive onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons either remains constant (V1b) or paradoxically increases (V1m) after MD, indicating that brief MD does not render the thalamocortical circuit less excitable.
evidence: This is inferred from the E-I ratio measurements showing no decrease or an increase.

claim: Loss of visual responsiveness in layer 4 V1m after brief MD during the critical period is due to a reconfiguration of intracortical circuits that leads to the recruitment of excess feedback inhibition.
source: Thus, feedforward and feedback E-I ratio onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons can be independently regulated by visual experience, and loss of visual responsiveness in layer 4 V1m after brief MD during the critical period is due to a reconfiguration of intracortical circuits that leads to the recruitment of excess feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the combination of experimental and modeling results.

claim: Manipulations that block thalamocortical LTD also prevent the reduction in layer 4 visual evoked potentials (VEPs) elicited by stimulation of the deprived eye.
source: Manipulations that block this LTD also prevent the reduction in layer 4 visual evoked potentials (VEPs) elicited by stimulation of the deprived eye (Yoon et al., 2009), an observation that led to the conclusion that LTD of thalamocortical inputs onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons is the primary mechanism for loss of visual responsiveness in layer 4 (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoon et al., 2009.

claim: The rapid negative-going VEP primarily measures direct thalamocortical-evoked synaptic responses.
source: However, the measure of visual responsiveness (the rapid negative-going VEP) used in Yoon et al., 2009 primarily measures direct thalamocortical-evoked synaptic responses (Rahmat, 2009; Khibnik et al., 2010), so is not expected to capture changes in intracortical circuitry or E-I ratio that might occur independently of thalamocortical LTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rahmat, 2009 and Khibnik et al., 2010.

claim: The reduced layer 4 VEP following brief MD reflects depression at both thalamocortical synapses onto pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons.
source: While we confirmed that brief MD induces LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons, we used paired recordings to show that synapses onto PV+ interneurons are more strongly depressed than synapses onto nearby pyramidal neurons, suggesting that the reduced layer 4 VEP following brief MD reflects depression at both synapse types.
evidence: This is inferred from the paired recording data showing differential depression.

claim: Enhancement of thalamocortical-evoked E-I ratio in V1m would produce an increase in network excitability if unopposed by other microcircuit changes.
source: In V1m, this in turn leads to an enhancement of thalamocortical-evoked E-I ratio onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (and thus net disinhibition of the feedforward thalamocortical circuit) that our modeling suggests would produce an increase in network excitability if unopposed by other microcircuit changes.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Intracortical inhibition is enhanced (relative to excitation) by brief MD.
source: Instead, our data strongly support an alternative explanation in which intracortical inhibition is enhanced (relative to excitation) by brief MD, and this enhancement suppresses the excitability of the layer 4 microcircuit.
evidence: This is supported by the intracortical E-I ratio measurements and modeling.

claim: Enhancement of intracortical inhibition suppresses the excitability of the layer 4 microcircuit.
source: Instead, our data strongly support an alternative explanation in which intracortical inhibition is enhanced (relative to excitation) by brief MD, and this enhancement suppresses the excitability of the layer 4 microcircuit.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In V1b as in V1m, there must be concurrent depression of disynaptic inhibition in the feedforward circuit.
source: Our data showing that thalamocortical E-I ratio in V1b stays constant following brief MD despite the well-documented depression of thalamocortical synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (Heynen et al., 2003; Crozier et al., 2007) strongly suggests that – in V1b as in V1m – there must be concurrent depression of disynaptic inhibition in the feedforward circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the constant E-I ratio despite documented thalamocortical depression.

claim: In neither barrel cortex nor V1b is the net excitability of the feedforward circuit reduced by brief MD.
source: Both barrel cortex and V1b receive convergent sensory inputs (from different whiskers or the two eyes, respectively), so it is possible that the differential regulation of feedforward E-I ratio in V1b and V1m reflects a tuning of the local plasticity mechanisms to these distinct characteristics of the sensory input. Importantly, in neither brain area is the net excitability of the feedforward circuit reduced by brief MD, indicating that other, presumably intracortical, changes must contribute to the loss of responsiveness to the deprived eye.
evidence: This is inferred from the E-I ratio measurements in both regions.

claim: Other, presumably intracortical, changes must contribute to the loss of responsiveness to the deprived eye in V1b.
source: Both barrel cortex and V1b receive convergent sensory inputs (from different whiskers or the two eyes, respectively), so it is possible that the differential regulation of feedforward E-I ratio in V1b and V1m reflects a tuning of the local plasticity mechanisms to these distinct characteristics of the sensory input. Importantly, in neither brain area is the net excitability of the feedforward circuit reduced by brief MD, indicating that other, presumably intracortical, changes must contribute to the loss of responsiveness to the deprived eye.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of feedforward circuit suppression.

claim: Thalamocortical inputs from the non-deprived eye are unchanged after 2–3 days of MD.
source: It is possible to measure thalamocortical E-I ratio in V1b with reasonable accuracy, because although only ~2/3 of labeled thalamocortical axons arise from the deprived eye, there is strong evidence that thalamocortical inputs from the non-deprived eye are unchanged after 2 – 3 days of MD (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Kaneko et al., 2008), so deprived-eye changes should still be detectible at these input synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frenkel and Bear, 2004 and Kaneko et al., 2008.

claim: Changes in intracortical inhibition are highly dynamic and depend critically on the neocortical region, the length of sensory deprivation, the source of inhibition, and the neocortical layer under investigation.
source: Many studies have examined the impact of sensory deprivation on PV+ fast spiking (FS) inhibition within primary sensory cortex, using a variety of protocols to elicit and measure inhibition (Hengen et al., 2013; House et al., 2011; Kannan et al., 2016; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2006; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014). Together, these studies suggest that changes in intracortical inhibition are highly dynamic and depend critically on the neocortical region, the length of sensory deprivation, the source of inhibition, and the neocortical layer under investigation (Hengen et al., 2013; Kannan et al., 2016; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2004, Maffei and Turrigiano, 2008, Maffei et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining inhibition after sensory deprivation.

claim: The same PV+ FS interneurons generate both feedforward and feedback inhibition within layer 4 and layer 2/3.
source: In part, this is due to the difficulty in isolating these two intimately related aspects of inhibition; the same PV+ FS interneurons generate both feedforward and feedback inhibition within layer 4 and layer 2/3 (Figure 1A), and many methods of evoking inhibition (for example electrical or visual stimulation) will elicit both together.
evidence: This is a description of established circuit architecture.

claim: In V1m, feedforward and feedback inhibitory microcircuit motifs change in opposite directions following brief MD.
source: Here we used an optogenetic approach to isolate and independently measure these two aspects of inhibition, and we found that in V1m these two distinct inhibitory microcircuit motifs – one mediated by thalamocortical drive and the other mediated by recurrent pyramidal drive onto the same postsynaptic PV+ interneurons – change in opposite directions following brief MD.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental measurements of feedforward and feedback E-I ratios.

claim: PV+ FS synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons are known to be plastic.
source: Although PV+ FS synapses onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons are known to be plastic (Lefort et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2004; Maffei et al., 2006; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014), changes at this synapse cannot account for either MD-induced increased feedforward or decreased feedback inhibition onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons, as we observed no change in either PV+ interneuron to pyramidal synaptic strength or in intrinsic excitability of PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lefort et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2004; Maffei et al., 2006; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014.

claim: Independent regulation of feedforward and feedback inhibition requires either that the sources of inhibition differ, or that the same source of inhibition is differentially recruited by feedforward and feedback excitatory drive.
source: Independent regulation of feedforward and feedback inhibition requires either that the sources of inhibition differ, or that the same source of inhibition is differentially recruited by feedforward and feedback excitatory drive.
evidence: This is a logical statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Brief MD induces strong depression of thalamocortical synapses onto PV+ interneurons while spontaneous mEPSCs onto PV+ cells are potentiated.
source: Our data support the latter model, as brief MD induces strong depression of thalamocortical synapses onto PV+ interneurons, while at the same time spontaneous mEPSCs (which largely arise from intracortical sources) onto PV+ cells are potentiated.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data from Figures 4 and 8.

claim: Under basal conditions, both feedforward and feedback inhibition in layer 4 are largely mediated by PV+ interneurons.
source: Under basal conditions, both feedforward and feedback inhibition in layer 4 are largely mediated by PV+ interneurons; although SST+ interneurons (the other major GABAergic cell type in layer 4) do inhibit pyramidal neurons, they receive relatively weak thalamocortical drive (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016) and provide much stronger inhibition onto PV+ FS interneurons than onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (Xu et al., 2013), and so they are thought to primarily disinhibit pyramidal neurons in layer 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2013.

claim: SST+ interneurons receive relatively weak thalamocortical drive.
source: Under basal conditions, both feedforward and feedback inhibition in layer 4 are largely mediated by PV+ interneurons; although SST+ interneurons (the other major GABAergic cell type in layer 4) do inhibit pyramidal neurons, they receive relatively weak thalamocortical drive (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016) and provide much stronger inhibition onto PV+ FS interneurons than onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (Xu et al., 2013), and so they are thought to primarily disinhibit pyramidal neurons in layer 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016.

claim: SST+ interneurons provide much stronger inhibition onto PV+ FS interneurons than onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons.
source: Under basal conditions, both feedforward and feedback inhibition in layer 4 are largely mediated by PV+ interneurons; although SST+ interneurons (the other major GABAergic cell type in layer 4) do inhibit pyramidal neurons, they receive relatively weak thalamocortical drive (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016) and provide much stronger inhibition onto PV+ FS interneurons than onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (Xu et al., 2013), and so they are thought to primarily disinhibit pyramidal neurons in layer 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: SST+ interneurons are thought to primarily disinhibit pyramidal neurons in layer 4.
source: Under basal conditions, both feedforward and feedback inhibition in layer 4 are largely mediated by PV+ interneurons; although SST+ interneurons (the other major GABAergic cell type in layer 4) do inhibit pyramidal neurons, they receive relatively weak thalamocortical drive (Beierlein et al., 2003; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016) and provide much stronger inhibition onto PV+ FS interneurons than onto layer 4 pyramidal neurons (Xu et al., 2013), and so they are thought to primarily disinhibit pyramidal neurons in layer 4.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger inhibition of SST+ cells onto PV+ interneurons.

claim: The shift toward enhanced intracortical inhibition outweighs the effects of reduced thalamocortical inhibition over a wide range of network parameters.
source: In this model, the shift toward enhanced intracortical inhibition outweighs the effects of reduced thalamocortical inhibition over a wide range of network parameters; this is in large part because the vast majority of input to both PV+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons arises from recurrent excitatory synapses, so that even small changes to net intracortical excitatory drive to inhibitory neurons can have a powerful impact on layer 4 firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 9D and 9E.

claim: The vast majority of input to both PV+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons arises from recurrent excitatory synapses.
source: In this model, the shift toward enhanced intracortical inhibition outweighs the effects of reduced thalamocortical inhibition over a wide range of network parameters; this is in large part because the vast majority of input to both PV+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons arises from recurrent excitatory synapses, so that even small changes to net intracortical excitatory drive to inhibitory neurons can have a powerful impact on layer 4 firing.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge cited earlier in the paper.

claim: Even small changes to net intracortical excitatory drive to inhibitory neurons can have a powerful impact on layer 4 firing.
source: In this model, the shift toward enhanced intracortical inhibition outweighs the effects of reduced thalamocortical inhibition over a wide range of network parameters; this is in large part because the vast majority of input to both PV+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons arises from recurrent excitatory synapses, so that even small changes to net intracortical excitatory drive to inhibitory neurons can have a powerful impact on layer 4 firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the numerical dominance of recurrent inputs and supported by modeling.

claim: Eyelid closure during MD leads to a degradation of retinal input to dLGN and the decorrelation of firing of dLGN relay neurons.
source: Eyelid closure during MD leads to a degradation of retinal input to dLGN and the decorrelation of firing of dLGN relay neurons (Linden et al., 2009), and this decorrelation likely drives LTD by reducing the ability of thalamocortical afferents to effectively cooperate to depolarize postsynaptic pyramidal neurons (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Linden et al., 2009.

claim: Decorrelation of dLGN firing likely drives LTD by reducing the ability of thalamocortical afferents to effectively cooperate to depolarize postsynaptic pyramidal neurons.
source: Eyelid closure during MD leads to a degradation of retinal input to dLGN and the decorrelation of firing of dLGN relay neurons (Linden et al., 2009), and this decorrelation likely drives LTD by reducing the ability of thalamocortical afferents to effectively cooperate to depolarize postsynaptic pyramidal neurons (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2009.

claim: The same MD-induced decorrelation of thalamocortical input that drives LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto pyramidal neurons is even more effective at driving LTD at synapses onto PV+ interneurons.
source: Our data suggest that the same MD-induced decorrelation of thalamocortical input that drives LTD at thalamocortical synapses onto pyramidal neurons is even more effective at driving LTD at synapses onto PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential depression observed in paired recordings.

claim: The imbalance in LTD induction results in an enhanced feedforward excitability, which may serve to compensate for degraded sensory input by boosting the sensitivity of the system to the input that remains.
source: This imbalance in LTD induction results in an enhanced feedforward excitability, which may serve to compensate for degraded sensory input by boosting the sensitivity of the system to the input that remains (Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional purpose of the observed changes, with citation to Hennequin et al., 2017.

claim: The change in feedback inhibitory charge is primarily driven by a prolongation of inhibitory current rather than a change in peak current.
source: Interestingly, unlike the change in feedforward inhibition in V1m (Figure 1G), the change in feedback inhibitory charge is primarily driven by a prolongation of inhibitory current rather than a change in peak current (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is observed from the waveforms shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The recruitment of inhibitory neurons by intracortical drive is prolonged after brief MD.
source: This suggests that the recruitment of inhibitory neurons by intracortical drive is prolonged after brief MD, presumably due to increased net excitation onto PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the prolongation of inhibitory current.

claim: Feedforward changes alone will enhance firing of both pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons and enhance synchrony.
source: For instance, our modeling predicts that feedforward changes alone will enhance firing of both pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons and enhance synchrony (Figure 9B), which could be sufficient to drive plasticity at intracortical synapses onto inhibitory neurons (Caporale and Dan, 2008; Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Enhanced firing and synchrony could be sufficient to drive plasticity at intracortical synapses onto inhibitory neurons.
source: For instance, our modeling predicts that feedforward changes alone will enhance firing of both pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons and enhance synchrony (Figure 9B), which could be sufficient to drive plasticity at intracortical synapses onto inhibitory neurons (Caporale and Dan, 2008; Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Caporale and Dan, 2008 and Hennequin et al., 2017.

claim: The increased feedforward E-I ratio should boost the ability of thalamic inputs to drive pyramidal neurons, thus offsetting to some extent the impact of degraded retinal drive.
source: The increased feedforward E-I ratio should boost the ability of thalamic inputs to drive pyramidal neurons, thus offsetting to some extent the impact of degraded retinal drive.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the observed changes.

claim: The prolongation of recurrent inhibition is expected to prevent signals from being amplified and spreading out in time and space.
source: Concurrently, the prolongation of recurrent inhibition is expected to prevent these signals from being amplified and spreading out in time and space.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the observed changes.

claim: These combined changes may constrain overall activity in layer 4 to prevent the amplification of noise, while still allowing the temporal pattern of thalamocortical input to influence layer 4 pyramidal spike patterns.
source: Thus, these changes together may constrain overall activity in layer 4 to prevent the amplification of noise, while still allowing the temporal pattern of thalamocortical input to influence layer 4 pyramidal spike patterns.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional purpose of the observed changes.
